A protest is an open, deliberate act of expressing strong disagreement with something a person — or a group of people — believes is wrong, unfair, or unjust. What separates a protest from a private opinion is that it is outward. It is not enough to feel that something is wrong; a protest happens when you make that feeling known — publicly, officially, or through deliberate action directed at whoever has the power to change the situation.

Think of it this way: if you quietly believe a new law is unjust but do nothing and say nothing about it, that is not a protest. The moment you stand up and openly declare "This is wrong and I object to it" — whether through words, a gathering, or a formal statement — that is a protest.

The two essential ingredients. For something to qualify as a protest, two things must come together: a genuine sense of disagreement or disapproval, and an outward expression that makes that disagreement visible to others. A protest without expression is just a private feeling. Expression without genuine conviction is just a comment. When both are present — and when they are directed at something the person believes is genuinely unjust — you have a protest.

Scale: from one person to millions. A protest can involve any number of people, and this is important to understand. A single individual can file a formal protest — say, writing to a company to officially declare that their treatment of a customer was unfair. A group of workers can stage a protest outside their employer's building. Thousands of people can gather in a city square to protest a government decision. Millions of people across multiple countries can march together in protest against war or climate change. The word scales freely from the deeply personal to the sweepingly global.

The many forms a protest takes. Protests do not look one way. A public demonstration — where people gather in streets, parks, or squares — is the most recognisable form. But a protest can also be a march (people walking together through public spaces to make their objection visible), a sit-in (people peacefully occupying a place and refusing to leave), a strike (workers halting their labour to protest against unjust pay or conditions), or a boycott (refusing to buy from or engage with something as an act of collective disapproval). Even a formal written statement filed with an authority — "We formally protest this decision" — is a protest in its clearest sense. All of these are correctly and accurately called a protest.

The phrase "under protest." This is one of the most important uses of this word you will encounter, and it reveals a quieter, more formal dimension of the word. When someone does something under protest, it means they are carrying out the action — but making it officially and clearly known that they object to having to do it. For example: "He signed the agreement under protest." He signed it — perhaps because he had no real choice — but he wanted it on the record that he considered it unfair. A protest, then, is not always a crowd or a march. Sometimes it is a calm, firm declaration: "I am doing this, but I want it known that I believe this is wrong."

The emotional and moral weight of the word. The word protest carries genuine moral weight. People protest because they believe something is genuinely wrong — not merely inconvenient or mildly annoying. It implies conviction: the belief that something crosses a clear line of fairness or justice. It implies courage, because standing up publicly or officially often involves personal risk. It implies passion, because you care enough to act rather than remain silent. And it almost always implies a desire for change — the person protesting wants the situation to be different. To say that someone protested something is to say they took a deliberate stand against it. It is not a neutral word.

The range of contexts in which you will see it. The word appears most commonly in political and social life — people protesting against laws, government decisions, war, discrimination, or inequality. But it is equally at home in the world of work, where employees stage protests against poor wages or dangerous conditions. It appears in sport, where a team or player might lodge a formal protest against a result they believe was reached unfairly. It appears in everyday life — a customer formally protesting a company's decision, or a citizen protesting a local planning ruling. Across all these contexts, the core meaning stays the same.

In one sentence. A protest is an open, deliberate expression — by one person or many — of strong disagreement with something believed to be wrong or unjust, made with the intention of being heard and, ultimately, of bringing about change.
